senses.gloss: Bold and willing to take big risks.
examples: It was an *audacious* plan to finish the bridge in two years.
The team pulled off an *audacious* comeback in the fourth quarter.

senses.gloss: Shocking or rude in a way that shows no respect.
examples: He made the *audacious* claim that he had never lost an argument.
That was the most *audacious* lie I've ever heard.

senses.gloss: Loud enough to be heard.
examples: Her voice was barely *audible* over the music.
There was an *audible* gasp from the audience.
The hum became more *audible* as we got closer to the machine.

senses.gloss: Using both sound and pictures.
examples: The school bought new *audiovisual* equipment for the auditorium.
Call the *audiovisual* department before your presentation.
The museum has an *audiovisual* display about the moon landing.

contrast: *auditory* is about the sense of hearing (*auditory problems*); *audible* means loud enough to be heard (*an audible sigh*).

senses.gloss: Relating to hearing.
examples: The *auditory* nerve carries signals from the ear to the brain.
Some children have trouble with *auditory* processing.
Loud concerts can cause lasting *auditory* damage.

senses.gloss: Made larger or more complete by adding something.
examples: The game uses *augmented* reality to put monsters on your street.
The orchestra played with an *augmented* string section.
This is an *augmented* version of last year's report.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an august institution*
contrast: The adjective is stressed on the second syllable (aw-GUHST); the month *August* is stressed on the first (AW-guhst) and written with a capital.

senses.gloss: Respected and impressive, often because of age or high rank.
examples: It is one of the most *august* universities in the country.
She was nervous speaking before such an *august* group of judges.
The club has an *august* history going back to 1850.

senses.gloss: Suggesting that something will be successful.
examples: It was an *auspicious* start to the season.
The timing didn't seem *auspicious*.
They couldn't have picked a more *auspicious* day for the wedding.

senses.gloss: Plain and simple, without decoration or comfort.
examples: The monks live in small, *austere* rooms.
The design of the building is clean and *austere*.

senses.gloss: Strict and serious in manner.
examples: Her grandfather was an *austere*, quiet man.
He was even more *austere* than his father.

senses.gloss: Involving sharp cuts in spending.
examples: The state passed an *austere* budget this year.
Voters were angry about the *austere* economic measures.

contrast: Always with a capital letter. Do not mix it up with *Austrian* (Austria, Vienna). *An Australian* is the noun for a person.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Australia.
examples: She has a strong *Australian* accent.
The *Australian* team won the gold medal.
My roommate is *Australian*.

contrast: *Austrian* is Austria (Vienna); *Australian* is Australia (Sydney). The words sound close.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Austria.
examples: Mozart was *Austrian*, not German.
We ate *Austrian* pastries at a café in Vienna.
The *Austrian* Alps are beautiful in winter.

senses.gloss: Real; not a copy or a fake.
examples: Experts say the painting is *authentic*.
Is this an *authentic* Rolex?

senses.gloss: Made or done in the traditional or original way.
examples: This is the most *authentic* Thai food in town.
The restaurant serves *authentic* Neapolitan pizza.

senses.gloss: True to one's own personality; sincere.
examples: Voters liked him because he seemed *authentic*.
She tries to be *authentic* on social media.

contrast: Russian *авторитетный* is *authoritative* (reliable, respected). *Authoritarian* is negative: demanding total obedience.

senses.gloss: Demanding strict obedience to the government and limiting people's freedom.
examples: The country has been under *authoritarian* rule for decades.
The government grew more *authoritarian* every year.

senses.gloss: Too strict with the people one controls, such as children or employees.
examples: He had an *authoritarian* father who never let him go out.
Her *authoritarian* style made the staff unhappy.

contrast: *authoritative* is positive (reliable, commanding respect); *authoritarian* is negative (demanding obedience).

senses.gloss: Reliable because it comes from an expert or official source.
examples: This is the most *authoritative* guide to birds in North America.
We need an *authoritative* answer from the IRS.

senses.gloss: Confident and commanding, so that people obey or respect you.
examples: She spoke in a calm, *authoritative* voice.
The coach has an *authoritative* manner with the players.

senses.gloss: Having official permission.
examples: *Authorized* personnel only.
Only managers are *authorized* to approve refunds.
Take your phone to an *authorized* repair shop.

contrast: A neutral medical description. Using it as an insult is offensive.

senses.gloss: Having autism.
examples: Their son is *autistic* and goes to a special program.
Many *autistic* adults work in tech.
The school offers extra support for *autistic* students.

senses.gloss: Based on or telling the story of the writer's own life.
examples: Her first novel is largely *autobiographical*.
The movie is based on an *autobiographical* essay he wrote in college.
His later songs became more *autobiographical*.

senses.gloss: Ruled by one person with unlimited power.
examples: The country is run by an *autocratic* regime.
The president became more *autocratic* after the election.

senses.gloss: Making decisions alone and expecting others to obey.
examples: Our old boss was *autocratic* and never asked for opinions.
Workers complained about his *autocratic* management style.

senses.gloss: Signed by the famous person who made, wrote or used it.
examples: He has an *autographed* baseball from the 1998 World Series.
The poster is *autographed* by the whole cast.
She sold her *autographed* copy of the book online.

senses.gloss: Caused by the body's immune system attacking its own cells.
examples: Lupus is an *autoimmune* disease.
She was diagnosed with an *autoimmune* disorder at thirty.
*Autoimmune* conditions are more common in women.

contrast: *automated* describes a process or system that machines now run instead of people (*an automated factory*); *automatic* describes a device that works by itself (*automatic doors*) or an action done without thinking.

senses.gloss: Done or run by machines or computers instead of people.
examples: The warehouse is almost fully *automated*.
You'll hear an *automated* message when you call.
Checkout at the grocery store is getting more *automated*.

contrast: It is also a noun: *She drives an automatic* (a car without a stick shift).

senses.gloss: Working by itself, without a person controlling it.
examples: The store has *automatic* doors.
Is your car *automatic* or stick shift?
The heater has an *automatic* shut-off switch.

senses.gloss: Done without thinking, out of habit.
examples: Saying thank you became *automatic* for her.
His reaction was *automatic*; he just ducked.

senses.gloss: Happening as a fixed result of a rule, with no decision needed.
examples: Cheating means *automatic* failure in this class.
There's an *automatic* fee for late payment.

contrast: *automotive* is for the car industry and car parts. For everyday things use the noun *car*: *a car trip*, not ✗ *an automotive trip*.

senses.gloss: Relating to cars and the business of making or repairing them.
examples: Detroit is the center of the American *automotive* industry.
He works at an *automotive* parts store.
She studied *automotive* engineering in college.

senses.gloss: Governing itself; independent of outside control.
examples: The region is *autonomous* but still part of the country.
Each department is fully *autonomous*.

senses.gloss: Able to operate without a human in control.
examples: The company is testing *autonomous* vehicles in Phoenix.
The farm uses *autonomous* tractors.

senses.gloss: Able to make one's own decisions and act alone.
examples: Teenagers want to be more *autonomous*.
The job suits *autonomous* workers who don't need a lot of supervision.

contrast: It is also a noun: *a hospital auxiliary* (a volunteer group), *an auxiliary* (a helping verb).

senses.gloss: Giving extra help or support; kept as a backup.
examples: The hospital has an *auxiliary* generator for power outages.
*Auxiliary* police help with traffic at big events.
*Do* and *have* can work as *auxiliary* verbs.

senses.gloss: Very new and experimental in art, music or fashion.
examples: The gallery shows mostly *avant-garde* art.
Her clothes are too *avant-garde* for most people.
His later films became even more *avant-garde*.

senses.gloss: Having a very strong desire for money and possessions.
examples: The *avaricious* landlord raised the rent again.
He grew more *avaricious* as he got richer.
The movie's villain is an *avaricious* banker.

senses.gloss: Relating to birds.
examples: Health officials are tracking a new strain of *avian* flu.
The zoo has a large *avian* exhibit.
Scientists study *avian* behavior in big cities.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an avid reader*

senses.gloss: Very enthusiastic about a hobby or interest.
examples: My dad is an *avid* golfer.
She's an *avid* reader of mystery novels.
He became a more *avid* fan after the team moved to town.

senses.gloss: Able to be prevented.
examples: The accident was completely *avoidable*.
Most of these injuries are *avoidable*.
It was an *avoidable* mistake.

senses.gloss: Openly stated or admitted.
examples: He is an *avowed* atheist.
Their *avowed* goal is to cut taxes.
She was an *avowed* enemy of the governor.

senses.gloss: Expected and wanted, often for a long time.
examples: The *long-awaited* sequel finally came out.
Her new album is eagerly *awaited*.
It's the most *awaited* game of the season.

senses.gloss: Covered with water.
examples: After the storm, the streets were *awash*.
The deck was *awash* with seawater.

senses.gloss: Having too much of something.
examples: The city is *awash* with tourists every summer.
Social media is *awash* in fake news.

senses.gloss: So impressive or beautiful that it fills you with wonder.
examples: The view from the rim of the Grand Canyon is *awe-inspiring*.
It was one of the most *awe-inspiring* performances I've ever seen.
They visited an *awe-inspiring* cathedral in Mexico City.

senses.gloss: Filled with wonder and respect.
examples: We stood in *awed* silence.
The kids were *awed* by the size of the dinosaur skeleton.
I was more *awed* than scared.

contrast: In everyday American speech *awesome* just means *great* (*That's awesome!*). The older meaning, causing awe, survives mainly in formal writing.

senses.gloss: Very good; great (informal).
examples: The concert was *awesome*!
You got the job? *Awesome*!
That was the most *awesome* weekend ever.

senses.gloss: So big, powerful or serious that it causes awe.
examples: We watched the *awesome* power of the ocean during the storm.
The president has an *awesome* responsibility.

senses.gloss: Filled with wonder and amazement.
examples: An *awestruck* child stared up at the fireworks.
She was completely *awestruck* by the Northern Lights.
The fans looked *awestruck* when the band walked in.

senses.gloss: Embarrassing and uncomfortable.
examples: There was an *awkward* silence after he said it.
It was the most *awkward* first date of my life.
I feel *awkward* around her parents.

senses.gloss: Not graceful; moving or behaving clumsily.
examples: He was a tall, *awkward* teenager.
She's a little *awkward* at parties.

senses.gloss: Difficult to handle, use or deal with.
examples: The box is an *awkward* shape to carry.
Friday afternoon is an *awkward* time for a meeting.

position: both — mostly after *go* or *be*: *He went AWOL*
form: acronym — *absent without leave*; also said letter by letter, A-W-O-L

senses.gloss: Absent from military duty without permission.
examples: Two soldiers went *AWOL* from the base.
He was *AWOL* for three weeks before they found him.

senses.gloss: Missing or gone when needed (informal).
examples: My roommate has been *AWOL* all weekend.
The TV remote has gone *AWOL* again.

contrast: Stress is on the second syllable and it rhymes with *cry*: uh-RY, not AW-ree.

senses.gloss: Wrong; not happening as planned.
examples: Our plans went *awry* when the car broke down.
Something had gone badly *awry* at the lab.

senses.gloss: Not straight; out of the normal position.
examples: His tie was *awry* after the long day.
Her hat was slightly *awry* from the wind.

senses.gloss: So obviously true that it does not need to be proved.
examples: It is *axiomatic* that more practice leads to better results.
For most economists, this principle is *axiomatic*.
She treats it as an *axiomatic* truth.

contrast: *Azeri* is a shorter synonym, used for the people and the language.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Azerbaijan.
examples: *Azerbaijani* cooking uses a lot of saffron.
The *Azerbaijani* capital is Baku.
Her grandparents were *Azerbaijani*.

senses.gloss: Bright blue, like a clear sky.
examples: The hotel overlooks the *azure* waters of the Caribbean.
Not a cloud crossed the *azure* sky.
The lake looked almost *azure* in the sunlight.

senses.gloss: Having a young-looking, round face like a child's.
examples: The *baby-faced* quarterback is actually thirty.
He looks *baby-faced*, but he's the oldest guy on the team.
A *baby-faced* actor played the young president.

senses.gloss: From or relating to ancient Babylon.
examples: The *Babylonian* king Hammurabi wrote one of the first law codes.
*Babylonian* astronomers tracked the movements of the planets.
Experts believe the clay tablet is *Babylonian*.

position: attributive only — *the back door*; after a verb use *at the back* or *in the back*
contrast: The adjective only goes before a noun: ✗ *The door is back* → *The door is in the back*. *Back* is much more often an adverb (*come back*), a noun (*my back hurts*) or a verb (*back up*).

senses.gloss: At or near the rear of something.
examples: Let's use the *back* door.
The kids sat in the *back* seat.
We had coffee on the *back* porch.

senses.gloss: From an earlier time; owed or published before now.
examples: He owes three years of *back* taxes.
The library keeps *back* issues of the magazine.

senses.gloss: Away from main roads and busy places.
examples: We took the *back* roads to avoid traffic.
They live on a quiet *back* street.

senses.gloss: Secret and unofficial, outside the normal channels.
examples: The two governments held *back-channel* talks for months.
She used her *back-channel* contacts to get the information.
The deal came out of *back-channel* negotiations.

contrast: As an adverb, written without hyphens, it means *with backs touching* (*stand back to back*) or *one after another* (*two games back to back*).

senses.gloss: Happening one right after the other.
senses.ru: идущие подряд, следующие друг за другом
examples: The Warriors won *back-to-back* championships.
I have *back-to-back* meetings all afternoon.
We had *back-to-back* snowstorms last week.

senses.gloss: Very hard and physically tiring.
examples: Picking cotton was *backbreaking* work.
The job was more *backbreaking* than I expected.
They spent a *backbreaking* summer building the barn.

senses.gloss: Seeming to praise but actually criticizing.
examples: 'You look great for your age' is a *backhanded* compliment.
She's an expert at *backhanded* praise.

senses.gloss: Done with the back of the hand facing forward.
examples: He hit a *backhanded* shot down the line.
She gave him a *backhanded* slap.

contrast: More common as an adverb, stressed on the second syllable: *We went backstage after the show*.

senses.gloss: Behind the stage, or private and out of public view.
examples: I got a *backstage* pass for the concert.
The documentary shows the *backstage* drama of a Broadway show.
There was a lot of *backstage* arguing before the deal was signed.

contrast: In American English the adjective is *backward*; *backwards* is only an adverb (*walk backwards*), and *backward* can be the adverb too. Calling people or places *backward* sounds insulting.

senses.gloss: Directed toward the back or the starting point.
examples: She took a *backward* step.
He left without a *backward* glance.

senses.gloss: Less developed or modern than others.
examples: The region was once one of the most *backward* in the state.
Some people still hold *backward* ideas about women.

senses.gloss: Caused by or relating to bacteria.
examples: Antibiotics only work on *bacterial* infections.
Strep throat is *bacterial*, not viral.
The lab tests water for *bacterial* growth.

senses.gloss: Behaving rudely; not polite.
examples: The *bad-mannered* guests left without saying goodbye.
It's *bad-mannered* to check your phone at dinner.
He was the most *bad-mannered* kid in the class.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed or angry.
examples: Our neighbor is a *bad-tempered* old man.
She gets *bad-tempered* when she's hungry.
The meeting got more *bad-tempered* as it went on.

contrast: *baffled* is the person who does not understand; *baffling* is the thing that causes it: *I was baffled by the baffling instructions*.

senses.gloss: Completely unable to understand something.
examples: Doctors were *baffled* by her symptoms.
He gave me a *baffled* look.
I'm even more *baffled* now than before.

contrast: *baffling* is the thing; *baffled* is the person who does not understand it.

senses.gloss: Impossible to understand or explain.
examples: The instructions were completely *baffling*.
Police called it a *baffling* case.
The most *baffling* part is that nobody saw anything.

senses.gloss: Hanging loosely, because it is too big.
examples: He wore *baggy* jeans and a hoodie.
My pants got *baggier* after I lost weight.
The sweater was a little *baggy* on him.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the Bahamas.
examples: We tried *Bahamian* conch fritters.
The *Bahamian* dollar is worth the same as the US dollar.
Her mother is *Bahamian*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Bahrain.
examples: The *Bahraini* government announced new visa rules.
He's *Bahraini* but lives in Houston.
*Bahraini* pearls were famous for centuries.

senses.gloss: Cooked in an oven with dry heat.
examples: I'll have a *baked* potato with sour cream.
Is the chicken fried or *baked*?
The church sells *baked* goods every Sunday.

contrast: An extreme adjective, so not *very baking hot*. Americans also just say *baking*: *It's baking out there!*

senses.gloss: Extremely hot.
examples: It was *baking hot* inside the car.
We spent a *baking hot* afternoon at the ballpark.
Don't leave the dog outside; it's *baking hot*.

senses.gloss: Having the right amounts of different things.
examples: Try to eat a *balanced* diet.
The team has a more *balanced* offense this year.

senses.gloss: Fair, giving all sides equal attention.
examples: The article gives a *balanced* view of the issue.
Viewers want *balanced* news coverage.

senses.gloss: Calm and sensible.
examples: She's a very *balanced* person.
He seems *well-balanced* despite everything he's been through.

senses.gloss: Having little or no hair on the head.
examples: My dad started going *bald* in his thirties.
He's *balder* than his older brother.
A *bald* man in a suit opened the door.

senses.gloss: Worn smooth or without the usual covering.
examples: You need new tires; these are *bald*.
The lawn has *bald* spots after the drought.

senses.gloss: Plain and direct, with nothing added to soften it.
examples: The report was a *bald* statement of the facts.
That's a *bald* lie.

contrast: Almost always *a bald-faced lie*. *Barefaced* means the same.

senses.gloss: Open and shameless, with no attempt to hide it.
examples: That's a *bald-faced* lie.
It was a *bald-faced* attempt to buy votes.
He told a *bald-faced* lie to the judge.

senses.gloss: Starting to lose the hair on the head.
examples: A *balding* man in his fifties sat next to me.
He's *balding* and a little overweight.
My uncle was already *balding* at twenty-five.

position: both — before a noun in the missile sense; after *go* in the angry sense

senses.gloss: Relating to missiles or bullets and how they fly.
examples: The country tested a *ballistic* missile.
Police sent the bullets for *ballistic* testing.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry, in *go ballistic* (informal).
examples: My mom went *ballistic* when she saw the phone bill.
The coach went *ballistic* at the referee.

contrast: The *l* is silent: BAH-mee.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly warm, of weather or air.
examples: It was a *balmy* evening in Miami.
The weather gets *balmier* as you drive south.
We had the *balmiest* February on record.

senses.gloss: Made with dark, sweet Italian vinegar.
examples: Drizzle the salad with *balsamic* vinegar.
The tomatoes come with a *balsamic* glaze.
She served the chicken with a *balsamic* reduction.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Baltic Sea or the countries around it.
examples: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the *Baltic* states.
The *Baltic* Sea freezes in some winters.
We took a cruise along the *Baltic* coast.

senses.gloss: Boring and ordinary, with nothing new.
examples: The lyrics are pretty *banal*.
We had a *banal* conversation about the weather.
His second book was even more *banal* than the first.

senses.gloss: Wrapped in a bandage.
examples: He came home with a *bandaged* hand.
Her knee was still *bandaged* a week after the fall.
A nurse checked the *bandaged* wound.

contrast: American informal. Not the same as *banged-up*, which means damaged or bruised.

senses.gloss: Excellent (informal).
examples: You did a *bang-up* job on the kitchen.
The team had a *bang-up* season.
They threw a *bang-up* party for his retirement.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Bangladesh.
examples: The *Bangladeshi* restaurants in Queens serve great curry.
He grew up in a *Bangladeshi* family in New York.
My coworker is *Bangladeshi*.

senses.gloss: Sure to make money.
examples: She's one of the most *bankable* stars in Hollywood.
Superhero movies are still *bankable*.
The investors didn't think the idea was *bankable*.

contrast: Say *go bankrupt*. *Bankrupt* is also a verb (*The lawsuit bankrupted them*) and a noun (*a bankrupt*).

senses.gloss: Officially unable to pay one's debts.
examples: The company went *bankrupt* in 2009.
A *bankrupt* airline left thousands of passengers stuck.

senses.gloss: Completely without a good quality.
examples: Critics called the government morally *bankrupt*.
The campaign is *bankrupt* of new ideas.

senses.gloss: Officially not allowed.
examples: The athlete tested positive for a *banned* substance.
Fireworks are *banned* in this county.
He's *banned* from the gym for a month.

contrast: Only before a noun, mostly *a banner year* or *a banner season*. The noun *banner* is a flag or a long sign.

senses.gloss: Unusually good or successful.
examples: It was a *banner* year for the company.
Farmers had a *banner* harvest.
The Braves are coming off a *banner* season.

senses.gloss: Having gone through the Christian ceremony of baptism.
examples: She's a *baptized* Catholic.
Only *baptized* members can take communion.
He was raised in the church but was never *baptized*.

contrast: The informal word is *Bajan*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Barbados.
examples: Rihanna is *Barbadian*.
*Barbadian* rum is famous around the world.
They flew the *Barbadian* flag at the festival.

senses.gloss: Extremely cruel and violent.
examples: Many people think the death penalty is *barbaric*.
It was a *barbaric* attack on civilians.
Conditions in the prison were even more *barbaric* than reported.

senses.gloss: Cooked slowly over a fire or on a grill, often with a sauce.
senses.ru: жаренный на гриле, приготовленный на барбекю
examples: We had *barbecued* ribs for dinner.
The chicken is *barbecued* over charcoal.
They sell *barbecued* corn at the fair.

senses.gloss: Having sharp points that stick out backward.
examples: The farm is surrounded by a *barbed* wire fence.
The hook is *barbed* so the fish can't get off.

senses.gloss: Meant to hurt someone's feelings.
examples: She made a *barbed* comment about his weight.
His jokes got more *barbed* as the night went on.

position: both — before a noun only in the sense 'the smallest amount'
contrast: Sounds exactly like *bear*. For 'naked' about a whole person Americans usually say *naked*; *bare* is for parts of the body and surfaces.

senses.gloss: Not covered by clothes or anything else.
examples: Don't walk on the hot sand in *bare* feet.
The trees were *bare* by November.
He slept on the *bare* floor.

senses.gloss: Empty; without the usual things.
examples: Store shelves were *bare* before the hurricane.
The apartment still had *bare* walls.

senses.gloss: Only the most basic; the smallest amount needed.
examples: We packed only the *bare* necessities.
He did the *bare* minimum to pass.
There wasn't even the *barest* hint of a smile.

senses.gloss: Fought with fists and no boxing gloves.
examples: *Bare-knuckle* boxing is legal in some states.
The two men got into a *bare-knuckle* fight outside the bar.

senses.gloss: Aggressive and without any rules or restraint.
examples: It was a *bare-knuckle* political campaign.
The firm is known for *bare-knuckle* business tactics.

contrast: More often an adverb: *She rode bareback*.

senses.gloss: Riding a horse without a saddle.
examples: *Bareback* riding is one of the toughest rodeo events.
The circus had a *bareback* rider in a sparkly costume.
The ranch offers *bareback* lessons for experienced riders.

contrast: Also an adverb (*walk barefoot*), with the same form. *Barefooted* exists but is less common.

senses.gloss: Not wearing shoes or socks.
examples: She was *barefoot* when she answered the door.
Two *barefoot* kids were playing in the yard.
Is it OK to go *barefoot* in here?

senses.gloss: Relating to air pressure or a barometer.
examples: *Barometric* pressure drops before a storm.
Changes in *barometric* pressure give me headaches.
The *barometric* reading was unusually low.

contrast: For the historical style it is often written with a capital: *Baroque music*.

senses.gloss: In the style of European art, buildings and music of about 1600 to 1750.
examples: We went to a concert of *baroque* music.
The church has a painted *baroque* ceiling.

senses.gloss: Too complicated or full of decoration.
examples: The tax rules are *baroque*.
His writing is even more *baroque* than his speeches.

takes: *from* + noun or *-ing*, in the sense 'not allowed'

senses.gloss: Having bars across it.
examples: The house has *barred* windows.
The door was *barred* from the inside.

senses.gloss: Not allowed to do something or go somewhere.
examples: He is *barred* from entering the country.
Reporters were *barred* from the meeting.

contrast: *Barren* for a woman who cannot have children is old-fashioned and now sounds offensive.

senses.gloss: Too dry or poor for plants to grow.
examples: The land around the town is flat and *barren*.
They drove through miles of *barren* desert.
The hills looked even more *barren* in winter.

senses.gloss: Producing no results or useful ideas.
examples: It was a *barren* period in her career.
The talks were *barren* of progress.

senses.gloss: Blocked or shut in behind a barrier.
examples: Police surrounded the *barricaded* house.
The streets were *barricaded* for the parade.
A *barricaded* suspect refused to come out.

contrast: Formal. *Base* is far more often a noun (*a military base*) or a verb (*based on*).

senses.gloss: Morally low; without honor.
examples: The ad appeals to people's *basest* instincts.
Greed is one of the *baser* human emotions.
He was driven by *base* motives.

senses.gloss: Of a metal: common and not valuable.
examples: Alchemists tried to turn *base* metals into gold.
The ring is a *base* metal with gold plating.

position: predicative only — before a noun only in compounds: *a Denver-based company*
contrast: ✗ *basing on the numbers* → *based on the numbers*.

senses.gloss: Having its main office or home in a place.
examples: The company is *based* in Seattle.
She works for a *Denver-based* startup.
Where are you *based*?

senses.gloss: Using something as the starting point or source.
examples: The movie is *based* on a true story.
Her decision was *based* on the facts.

senses.gloss: Not supported by any facts.
examples: The accusations are completely *baseless*.
He spread *baseless* rumors about his rival.
The judge threw out the *baseless* lawsuit.

senses.gloss: Shy and easily embarrassed.
examples: He gave her a *bashful* smile.
Don't be *bashful*; come say hi.
She was more *bashful* than her sisters.

contrast: Russian *основной* often means *main* (*the main idea*), not *basic*. *Basic* is 'the simplest, necessary level'.

senses.gloss: Forming the main or most necessary part.
examples: Food and shelter are *basic* human needs.
First learn the *basic* rules of the game.

senses.gloss: Simple, with nothing extra.
examples: The hotel room was pretty *basic*.
I only know some *basic* Spanish.
This is the most *basic* model they sell.

senses.gloss: Ordinary and unoriginal, following popular trends (slang).
examples: Pumpkin spice lattes? That's so *basic*.
She thinks his taste in music is kind of *basic*.

senses.gloss: Changed in a way that makes it worse than the original.
examples: The restaurant serves a *bastardized* version of Italian food.
The movie is a *bastardized* version of the novel.
Over the years the song became more and more *bastardized*.

senses.gloss: Old and damaged from a lot of use.
examples: He drives a *battered* old pickup.
My copy of the book is more *battered* than yours.

senses.gloss: Hurt by repeated violence.
examples: The shelter helps *battered* women and their children.
The *battered* boxer could barely stand.

senses.gloss: Covered in batter and fried.
examples: We ordered *battered* shrimp.
The fish is *battered* and deep-fried.

senses.gloss: Getting its power from a battery.
examples: I bought a *battery-powered* lawn mower.
The lamp is *battery-powered*, so you can use it outside.
*Battery-powered* cars are getting cheaper.

senses.gloss: Damaged or marked by fighting or long struggle.
examples: A *battle-scarred* veteran spoke at the ceremony.
The *battle-scarred* city is slowly rebuilding.
After the long campaign, the senator looked tired and *battle-scarred*.
